## Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use [breast-cancer.csv](data/breast-cancer.csv), which contains 569 cases from the [Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast%2Bcancer%2Bwisconsin%2Bdiagnostic). Predict `y` (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using `mean_radius`, `mean_texture`, and `mean_smoothness`.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$
k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.
$$

Using the estimated probabilities for `y = 1` on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

I use the supplied 70/30 split in `data/breast-cancer-split.csv` (398 training, 171 test), so there is no random component and no seed is needed.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

data = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")
split = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer-split.csv")
assert (split["row"].to_numpy() == np.arange(1, len(data) + 1)).all()   # rows match by position

features = ["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]
is_train = (split["split"] == "train").to_numpy()
X, y = data[features].to_numpy(), data["y"].to_numpy()

mean, sd = X[is_train].mean(axis=0), X[is_train].std(axis=0, ddof=0)   # training statistics only
X_train, X_test = (X[is_train] - mean) / sd, (X[~is_train] - mean) / sd
y_train, y_test = y[is_train], y[~is_train]

models = {"Logistic": LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=10000)}
for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]:
    models[f"KNN k={k}"] = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", algorithm="brute")

styles = ["-", "--", "--", "--", "--", "--"]
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 5))
auc_rows = []
for (name, model), ls in zip(models.items(), styles):
    p_test = model.fit(X_train, y_train).predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, p_test)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test)
    auc_rows.append((name, auc))
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, ls, lw=2 if name == "Logistic" else 1.3, label=f"{name} (AUC {auc:.3f})")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", lw=0.7, linestyle=":")
plt.xlabel("False positive rate"); plt.ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.title("Test ROC curves"); plt.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

pd.DataFrame(auc_rows, columns=["model", "test AUC"]).round(4)
```

I prefer logistic regression: it has the highest test AUC ($0.975$), though KNN with $k=45$ is essentially tied ($0.974$). KNN improves steadily with $k$ (from $0.933$ at $k=5$), since larger neighborhoods smooth the noisy probability estimates. Given the near-tie on 171 test cases, logistic regression wins on simplicity: no tuning parameter and interpretable coefficients.

## Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$
k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.
$$

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its $k$ nearest neighbors.

For each $k$, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with $k$. In particular, explain what happens at $k=1$ and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Same split and standardization as Question 1.

```{python}
ks = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3.4), sharey=True)
rows = []
for ax, k in zip(axes, ks):
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", algorithm="brute").fit(X_train, y_train)
    # predicting on the training data keeps each observation among its own k neighbors
    for label, Xs, ys, color in [("train", X_train, y_train, "C0"), ("test", X_test, y_test, "C1")]:
        p = knn.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1]
        fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(ys, p)
        auc = roc_auc_score(ys, p)
        rows.append((k, label, auc))
        ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=color, label=f"{label} (AUC {auc:.3f})")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", lw=0.7, linestyle=":")
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}"); ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate"); ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["k", "set", "AUC"]).pivot(index="k", columns="set", values="AUC")[["train", "test"]].round(4)
```

Training AUC is higher than test AUC for every $k$, and the gap shrinks as $k$ grows (from $1.000$ vs. $0.876$ at $k=1$ to $0.988$ vs. $0.959$ at $k=20$). At $k=1$ each training point's single nearest neighbor is itself, so its predicted probability is exactly its own label and the training ROC is perfect regardless of how well the model generalizes. Larger $k$ dilutes the self-match, so the training fit becomes less optimistic. Training performance does not reflect new observations because the model has already seen the training labels; only the test curve measures performance on unseen cases.
